note: Original lab explanations and report-reading questions, with independently checked aggregate calculations. Obtain the official workbooks and answer keys from Virtuale.

guides.title: OECD: describe countries, then investigate outliers
guides.citation: Descriptive Statistics LAB, data described as 2019; raw worksheet DP_LIVE_27092023160309805, rows 2–39; answer workbook Answers and Sheet1.
guides.unit: One country; seven variables with different units.
guides.goal: Build a reproducible descriptive table and explain how missing values and flagged observations affect it.

steps.title: Define the observations
steps.text: There are 38 country rows, not 38 patients. Select rows 2–39. Excel’s formatted last row is not a sample-size definition. These are unweighted country summaries, not averages for a randomly sampled person.

steps.title: Count each variable separately
steps.text: COUNT ignores blank cells but keeps numerical zeros. The seven columns have n=38, 38, 32, 38, 27, 25 and 37. Do not divide every sum by 38 or replace missing data by zero.

steps.title: Name the quartile convention
steps.text: Use QUARTILE.INC for the workbook comparison. Q1−1.5×IQR and Q3+1.5×IQR are fences. Whiskers are the most extreme observed values inside those fences. The slide np convention can produce different quartiles.

steps.title: Investigate, then show sensitivity
steps.text: Compare the full data with a variable-specific calculation excluding values strictly outside the fences. This is a sensitivity exercise, not permission to erase observations. Removing an entire country across all variables is a different analysis.

tables.title: Checked full-data descriptive summaries (SD uses n)

formulas.label: Count / mean / descriptive SD of SUICIDE (column C)
Mean inside SUICIDE fences, using the answer Sheet1 layout

cautions: Answer Sheet1!B42 uses >upper and <lower simultaneously, and includes summary rows C2:C100; its cached result is #DIV/0!. Use the raw rows and correctly oriented inclusive fence conditions.

CHILDVACCIN’s inclusive lower fence is 83.1375. Mexico (82), Brazil and Argentina (83) are all below it. The supplied outlier list omits Mexico. Removing all three gives n=35 and mean=94.9057%; the answer workbook retains Mexico, while the Word filtered table gives another result.

Costa Rica’s CHILDVACCIN value of 102.6% needs a definition/denominator or data-quality check even though it is inside the IQR fences. Statistical flags and plausible ranges answer different questions.

Some lower-fence inequalities in the Word answer table have an extra minus sign. For LIFEEXP, for example, the lower fence is +68.4875 years. The “largest/smallest non-outlying value” headings actually label calculated fences.

questions.prompt: Why does MEDICALDOC have n=25 when there are 38 countries?
options: Thirteen entries are missing; count numerical observations in this column
All missing values represent zero doctors
COUNT must include the country-name header
questions.explanation: The effective n is variable-specific. Missing values are unknown, while zero is an observed numerical value.

questions.prompt: CHILDVACCIN’s lower fence is 83.1375. Which treatment of Mexico’s value 82 follows the stated rule?
options: Keep it because the answer list omits Mexico
Flag it as below the fence and investigate before deciding what to exclude
Replace it with the sample mean without reporting the change
questions.explanation: 82 < 83.1375. The omission in the supplied answer list does not change the numerical rule; outlier status still does not establish a data error.

guides.title: Food spending: from an Excel column to a 90% interval
guides.citation: Inferential Statistics LAB; Food.xlsx, Data!A2:D51. Checked independently from all 50 numerical rows.
guides.unit: One randomly sampled adult; weekly spending in pounds (£).
guides.goal: Estimate the population means for fruit, vegetables and meat, and the population variance of total expenditure.

steps.title: Keep the right range
steps.text: Data rows are 2–51. B is exp_Fruit, C is exp_Veg, D is exp_Meat; the task’s exp_meet spelling refers to that last column. Keep the two fruit zeros, two vegetable zeros and four meat zeros: no spending is a valid observation.

steps.title: Separate sample spread from precision
steps.text: Calculate x̄ and s using STDEV.S. Use SE=s/√50 for uncertainty about the population mean, not s itself. For population variance of total expense, use VAR.S(A2:A51).

steps.title: Allocate the two tails
steps.text: For 90% confidence, α=.10 and α/2=.05. With unknown σ, use T.INV(.95,49)=1.6765509. Each interval is x̄±1.6765509×SE.

steps.title: Write a population-level conclusion
steps.text: The fruit interval estimates the population mean weekly fruit spending, not the range containing 90% of adults. The lab states random sampling. Spending is right-skewed; at n=50 the t procedure is a large-sample approximation unless population normality is justified.

tables.title: Checked 90% mean intervals; df=49; values in £
Two different variance targets for total spending

cautions: The three category intervals use the same 50 adults. They are individually 90% intervals, not a guaranteed simultaneous 90% statement about all three means.
Total expense is not defined here as just the sum of the three displayed categories. Use column A directly. Variance has squared currency units.
Do not test population variance: the lab asks for a point estimate, and variance hypothesis tests are outside this course’s stated scope.

questions.prompt: Which Excel critical value gives the requested two-sided 90% interval?
options: NORM.S.INV(0.90)
questions.explanation: Unknown σ means an estimated SE; df=n−1=49. The two tails each receive .05, so the positive critical quantile is .95.

questions.prompt: A participant reports £0 on meat. What should happen to this row?
options: Delete it as missing
Replace it by the mean
Keep it as a valid zero-spending observation
questions.explanation: A numerical zero is not a missing value. Deleting it would change both the target description and n.

guides.title: Variance: why n and n−1 give different answers
files: Exercise Variance and Adjusted Variance_ with answers.xlsx
guides.citation: Both workbooks, Data!B2:B9; answer sheet checks squared deviations and VAR.P / VAR.S.
guides.unit: Eight cholesterol measurements; the workbook does not state a measurement unit.
guides.goal: Reconcile manual squared deviations with Excel and choose the denominator for the question.

steps.title: Calculate one shared numerator
steps.text: For the eight measurements, x̄=170.25 and Σ(xᵢ−x̄)²=4537.5. Centre every deviation on the same mean.

steps.title: Describe the observed data
steps.text: Divide by 8: Vₙ=567.1875. This is the descriptive variance of the entered observations.

steps.title: Estimate population variance
steps.text: Divide by 7: S²=648.2142857. Under independent sampling, S² is unbiased for σ² across repeated samples. It is not guaranteed equal to σ² in this particular sample.

steps.title: Check the relationship and units
steps.text: S²=(8/7)×Vₙ. Adjusted SD=√S²=25.4601, in the original units; variance is in squared units. s itself is generally not unbiased for σ.

formulas.label: Squared deviation in D2; copy down

cautions: The dollar signs lock the mean cell when the formula is copied. Without them, later rows can subtract different cells.
Excel’s names do not require that the observed eight values form a complete real population for VAR.P to describe them. The intended target determines n versus n−1.

questions.prompt: For n=8 and the same squared-deviation sum, S²/Vₙ equals…
questions.explanation: S²=SS/7 and Vₙ=SS/8, giving S²/Vₙ=8/7.

questions.prompt: If the observations are measured in units U, VAR.S is measured in…
options: U
No units
U²
questions.explanation: Squaring deviations squares the unit. Taking the square root returns the original unit for SD.

guides.title: Two cholesterol samples: same mean, different spread
guides.citation: Sheet1!B3:B7 (sample 1) and H3:H7 (sample 2). This file differs from the Exercise Book CHOLESTEROL.xlsx.
guides.unit: Five measurements per sample; the workbook does not specify the cholesterol unit.
guides.goal: Explain why identical means do not make distributions identical.

steps.title: Check both centres
steps.text: Both means equal 200. That statement alone says nothing about their dispersion or shape.

steps.title: Keep denominators consistent
steps.text: Descriptive variances are 272 and 31.6; adjusted variances are 340 and 39.5. Each adjusted result is 5/4 times its descriptive result.

steps.title: Compare spread in original units
steps.text: Descriptive SDs are 16.4924 and 5.6214. Sample 1 is much more dispersed even though both means agree.

steps.title: Ask about design before inference
steps.text: Equal sample sizes do not establish pairing. The workbook does not specify a before/after or matched design. With n=5 per group, do not plug these values into the course large-sample independent z recipe.

cautions: Do not interpret the mean as a complete description of clinical variability.
Do not infer a paired design from matching row numbers, and do not infer equality of population means from equal observed means.

questions.prompt: Both sample means are 200. Which conclusion is supported?
options: The samples have identical distributions
The observed centres agree, but their spreads differ
The population means must be exactly equal
questions.explanation: Sample 1’s descriptive variance is 272 versus 31.6 for sample 2. Matching observed means cannot establish identical distributions or exact population equality.

questions.prompt: Can equal n=5 establish a paired design?
options: Yes: equal n always means paired
Yes: all two-column workbooks are paired
No: pairing must come from how measurements are linked
questions.explanation: Pairing is a design property, such as repeated measurements on the same people. It is not implied by equal counts.

guides.title: Birthweight and estriol: preserve the pairs
guides.unit: A linked birthweight–estriol record; birthweight in kg, estriol unit not specified.
guides.goal: Calculate and interpret covariance and correlation without losing the row pairing.

steps.title: Keep one shared set of rows
steps.text: Use the 15 complete paired records. Sorting one column independently would destroy the relationship between the two measurements.

steps.title: Measure association
steps.text: Covariance with n is 1.2111111; with n−1 it is 1.2976190. Correlation is 0.7175049 with either consistently matched convention.

steps.title: Interpret the direction
steps.text: Larger estriol values tend to accompany larger birthweights in these records. Pearson r measures linear association; it is dimensionless.

steps.title: Keep the claim within the design
steps.text: Correlation does not establish that changing estriol causes a change in birthweight. A scatterplot in Excel helps check shape and influential observations before relying on a single coefficient.

formulas.label: Excel scatterplot
formulas.formula: Select the two matched numeric columns → Insert → Scatter; label both axes and their stated units.

cautions: Do not mix covariance using n with SDs using n−1 in a manual formula for r.
Do not report an estriol unit that the supplied workbook does not define. Regression inference is outside this guide’s calculation scope.

questions.prompt: What happens if you sort only the estriol column?
options: The original pairs can be broken, altering the association
Correlation is always unchanged by independently sorting columns
It proves a causal relationship
questions.explanation: Correlation uses corresponding (xᵢ,yᵢ) records. Only sorting complete rows together preserves those pairs.

questions.prompt: Which reading of r≈0.7175 is justified?
options: Estriol causes exactly 71.75% of birthweight
There is positive linear association in these 15 records
71.75% of individual birthweights equal their mean
questions.explanation: The coefficient describes linear association. It is not a causal fraction, a percentage of equal observations, or an effect measured in kg.

guides.title: Otitis counts: expected value and discrete tails
guides.citation: Sheet1!A2:A8 (counts 0–6) and B2:B8 (probabilities). Upload uses the spelling Othitis.
guides.unit: A discrete count X under the supplied probability model.
guides.goal: Check a probability distribution, calculate moments and distinguish ≥ from >.

steps.title: Validate the probability model
steps.text: The listed probabilities are nonnegative and sum to 1. This is a probability table, not seven equally weighted observations.

steps.title: Weight each possible count
steps.text: E(X)=Σx×P(X=x)=2.038. An expected count need not itself be a possible individual count.

steps.title: Compute spread using moments
steps.text: E(X²)=6.12; Var(X)=6.12−2.038²=1.966556. Do not square the sum as a substitute for summing squared values.

steps.title: Respect the endpoint
steps.text: P(X≥3)=0.336 includes the probability at 3. P(X>3)=0.151 excludes it. Their difference is P(X=3)=0.185.

cautions: AVERAGE(A2:A8) weights all counts equally; it is not E(X) for this model.
The worksheet is a model distribution, not a sample from which to calculate VAR.S or a confidence interval.

questions.prompt: Why do P(X≥3)=.336 and P(X>3)=.151 differ?
options: The first includes P(X=3)=.185
The two probabilities should always agree
The distribution is continuous
questions.explanation: A discrete random variable can put positive mass at a single endpoint. ≥ includes 3, while > excludes it.

questions.prompt: Can E(X)=2.038 be valid for integer-valued X?
options: No: all expectations must be integers
Yes: the long-run weighted average need not be an individual possible value
Only if X is normally distributed
questions.explanation: An expectation is a probability-weighted average, not a requirement that one observation equal that value.

guides.title: All 25 samples: see bias and precision exactly
files: List of 25 independent samples from a 5 units population (2).xlsx
guides.citation: Worksheet’s 25 ordered pairs, rows 2–26. Population values match the existing exact-sampling experiment.
guides.unit: Two independent draws with replacement from the five-value population {8,4,2,11,6}.
guides.goal: Read all possible samples as an exact sampling distribution, not 25 new empirical study participants.

steps.title: Identify the sampling design
steps.text: There are 5×5=25 equally likely ordered outcomes. (8,4) and (4,8) are distinct outcomes, and (8,8) is allowed because sampling is with replacement.

steps.title: Calculate the population quantities
steps.text: The population has μ=6.2 and σ²=9.76. Averaging the 25 possible sample means gives 6.2: X̄ is unbiased for μ.

steps.title: See precision improve
steps.text: For n=2 independent draws, Var(X̄)=9.76/2=4.88. This is the variability of possible sample means, not the spread of the five individuals.

steps.title: Compare variance estimators
steps.text: Across these 25 outcomes, average descriptive sample variance Vₙ is 4.88, while average adjusted S² is 9.76. The latter matches the population variance. Without replacement, the design and resulting mean variance change.

formulas.label: Sample mean for each B,C pair
Across the enumeration
formulas.formula: AVERAGE of all 25 calculated means; VAR.P of those means; AVERAGE of each estimator column.

cautions: The file enumerates possible samples. It does not demonstrate that 25 collected samples happened to be independent experiments.
Sampling without replacement excludes duplicate draws and changes covariance. Do not reuse σ²/n without checking the design.

questions.prompt: Why are there 25 outcomes rather than 10?
options: The draws are ordered and replacement is allowed
The population has 25 people
The second draw cannot equal the first
questions.explanation: Five choices for the first draw and five for the second make 25 ordered outcomes. Ten is the number of unordered size-two subsets without replacement.

questions.prompt: Which average matches the population variance 9.76 in this enumeration?
options: Average descriptive Vₙ
Variance of the possible sample means
Average adjusted S²
questions.explanation: Average S² equals 9.76. Average Vₙ and Var(X̄) both equal 4.88 here, for different reasons.

guides.title: Health-centre visits: define the denominator
guides.citation: NCHS, National Health Statistics Reports No. 211, Visits to Health Centers Among Adults, by Selected Characteristics: United States, 2022 (22 October 2024), Table 1, PDF p. 7; methods pp. 2–3.
guides.unit: Percentage of adult health-centre visits in 2022, not percentage of unique people.
guides.goal: Read a survey percentage and interval while checking what a row and its denominator represent.

steps.title: Start with the statistical unit
steps.text: The unit is a visit. Repeat visits by one person can appear in the year’s data. The analytic file has 4,612,644 adult visits; weighting estimates 89.5 million visits.

steps.title: Distinguish proportions from visit rates
steps.text: 65.2% is the estimated share of adult visits made by women. It does not mean 65.2% of women attended a health centre. The report also gives visit rates per 1,000 people, a different quantity.

steps.title: Read the method and missingness
steps.text: 64 of 255 contacted centres participated (25.1%). Weights address selection and nonresponse; they do not by themselves guarantee absence of bias. Denominators vary with missing characteristics; marital status uses a smaller analytic subset.

steps.title: Read the legend before the stars
steps.text: Asterisks in this report flag unreliable estimates. They are not ordinary p-value stars. Several condition categories overlap, so their percentages need not sum to 100%.

cautions: Use the report’s design-based intervals. The large number of visits does not justify rebuilding them with a simple independent-binomial formula.
These rows describe visits to health centres. They cannot be generalized to all US healthcare use or all unique adult patients.

questions.prompt: The women row is 65.2% [63.7,66.7]. What is the estimated quantity?
options: The share of women who visited any doctor
The share of adult health-centre visits made by women
The share of all US women who are ill
questions.explanation: The denominator is adult visits in the specified health-centre setting and year, not women in the general population.

questions.prompt: What does an asterisk mean in this report’s tables?
options: An unreliable estimate under the reporting standard
Always p<.05
A causal effect
questions.explanation: The legend defines the symbol. Star conventions must be checked in each source.

intervals.label: Women
intervals.meaning: An estimated 65.2% of adult health-centre visits were made by women; the 95% interval is 63.7%–66.7%.

intervals.label: Men
intervals.meaning: An estimated 34.8% of adult visits were made by men; this is a visit share, not the chance that a man attends.

intervals.label: Age 18–44
intervals.meaning: An estimated 42.8% of adult visits were in the 18–44 age group.

intervals.label: Age 65+
intervals.meaning: An estimated 19.9% of adult visits were in the age-65-and-older group.

guides.intervalNote: Selected Table 1 rows; sex and age are separate classifications, so do not add all four rows. Published 95% endpoints are retained.

guides.title: Medication use: proportions in a complex survey
guides.citation: NCHS, National Health Statistics Reports No. 209, Prescription Medication Use, Coverage, and Nonadherence Among Adults Age 65 and Older: United States, 2021–2022 (5 September 2024), Table 1, PDF p. 8; methods pp. 2–3.
guides.unit: Percentage of US civilian noninstitutionalized adults aged 65+ reporting prescription use in the past 12 months.
guides.goal: Interpret a population proportion and recognize why its survey interval differs from a classroom Wald interval.

steps.title: Define eligibility and time
steps.text: The estimate concerns adults 65+ and use during the past 12 months. The pooled 2021–2022 NHIS sample has 17,706 such adults; it excludes institutionalized adults.

steps.title: Separate related outcomes
steps.text: Prescription use (88.6% overall) is not prescription coverage or a cost-related nonadherence measure. Read the outcome definition before comparing percentages.

steps.title: Use the reported uncertainty
steps.text: The 95% intervals use Korn–Graubard methods; SUDAAN accounts for the complex survey design. A classroom Wald interval based only on n=17,706 does not reproduce this calculation.

steps.title: Check comparison policy
steps.text: Individual tests use p<.05 without adjustment for multiple comparisons. Several comparisons therefore need more cautious reading than a single pre-specified test.

cautions: Intervals concern a proportion, not average doses or the share of all US adults using medicines.
Association of nonadherence with food insecurity in this observational survey does not alone establish causation.

questions.prompt: What does [88.1%,89.2%] estimate?
options: The population proportion of eligible older adults reporting prescription use
A range containing 95% of individual medication doses
A 95% probability that any selected individual takes medicine
questions.explanation: This is uncertainty about a population proportion under the survey procedure, not a distribution of doses or an individual prediction.

questions.prompt: Why should you keep the published interval instead of rebuilding a simple Wald one?
options: Survey weighting always removes all bias
Its variance and endpoints account for a complex survey design
A confidence interval has no connection to sampling
questions.explanation: The report uses design-aware variance and Korn–Graubard intervals. The simple independent-sample course formula is not the reported method.

intervals.label: All aged 65+
intervals.meaning: Estimated prescription use is 88.6%; the reported 95% interval for that population proportion is 88.1%–89.2%.

intervals.label: Age 65–74
intervals.meaning: The estimated proportion reporting use among ages 65–74 is 86.9%.

intervals.label: Age 75–84
intervals.meaning: The estimated proportion among ages 75–84 is 91.3%.

intervals.label: Age 85+
intervals.meaning: The estimated proportion among ages 85+ is 91.2%; its interval is wider than the overall interval.

guides.intervalNote: Selected Table 1 rows; the overall row contains the age subgroups. The axis starts at 80% to make interval widths readable; it is not a zero-based percentage bar chart.

guides.title: PISA: mean, SE and a dependent comparison
guides.citation: Measuring Up: Canadian Results of the OECD PISA 2022 Study, Box 1 PDF p. 27 (printed p. 13), Table B.1.2 PDF p. 126 (printed p. 112), Appendix A PDF pp. 115–120.
guides.unit: Mean mathematics score for participating populations of 15-year-old students; education example for reading mean CIs.
guides.goal: Distinguish individual spread from uncertainty in a mean and inspect a comparison whose groups overlap.

steps.title: Recognize the sample design
steps.text: Around 23,000 Canadian students participated. School/student sampling and weights differ from a simple random sample of independent patients. Appendix A identifies possible student nonresponse bias; estimates for Canada and seven provinces need caution.

steps.title: Separate SD from SE
steps.text: The report describes individual-score SD around 100, but Canada’s mean has SE=1.6. Individual variability and uncertainty in a weighted mean answer different questions.

steps.title: Read the rounded interval
steps.text: Canada’s mean is 497 with published 95% CI [494,500]. The rounded arithmetic 497±1.96×1.6 gives about [493.864,500.136], consistent after rounding. Published SEs also account for measurement uncertainty.

steps.title: Identify an overlapping comparison
steps.text: Canada includes Quebec, so these means are not independent. Table B.1.2 reports Quebec−Canada=17 with SE=3.6. Use the reported contrast SE, rather than √(3.9²+1.6²).

cautions: The report’s tables use stars to distinguish reference comparisons (OECD or Canada). Read the specific legend; three stars are not automatically p<.001 here.
Nonresponse adjustment does not establish representativeness without limitations. The report accepts the data with explicit caution; observed changes do not establish a causal COVID effect.

questions.prompt: Canada has mean=497 and SE=1.6. Which interpretation is correct?
options: Individual scores mostly lie within 1.6 points of 497
SE describes uncertainty in the estimated mean
SE is the largest observed student score
questions.explanation: SE concerns the estimator’s variability; individual scores have much larger dispersion.

questions.prompt: Why is the course independent-groups SE unsuitable for Quebec minus Canada?
options: Quebec is part of Canada, so the two means share observations
The mean of Quebec is larger
Both results have three digits
questions.explanation: Overlapping observations induce dependence. The table provides a design-appropriate contrast SE=3.6.

intervals.label: Canada
intervals.meaning: The estimated Canadian population mean mathematics score is 497; its reported 95% interval is 494–500.

intervals.label: Alberta
intervals.meaning: Alberta’s mean is 504 with a wider interval, 492–515. The highest point estimate alone does not settle a comparison.

intervals.label: Quebec
intervals.meaning: Quebec’s mean is 514. For Quebec−Canada, read the separately reported difference 17 and SE 3.6.

intervals.label: Ontario
intervals.meaning: Ontario’s mean is 495 with interval 489–501.

guides.intervalNote: Selected Table B.1.2 rows. Endpoints, means and SEs are rounded in the source. Province-versus-Canada comparisons are dependent.

guides.title: Health systems: intervals do not make a league table
guides.citation: OECD / The Health Foundation (2025), How Do Health System Features Influence Health System Performance?, Table 2.1 PDF p. 23 (printed p. 21); Figure 2.6 p. 24; Table 2.3 p. 26. DOI: 10.1787/7b877762-en. Selected numerical rows and original teaching plot; source CC BY 4.0, no endorsement implied.
guides.unit: Mean DEA efficiency score across countries in each institutional cluster, where 1 is the highest score.
guides.goal: Read interval uncertainty and formal contrasts before comparing clusters or claiming causation.

steps.title: Identify the level of analysis
steps.text: The observations are countries grouped by institutional features, not patient groups. DEA efficiency scores and clustering are report context, beyond the course’s required calculations.

steps.title: Compare precision as well as estimates
steps.text: Cluster 2 has a point estimate .71 [ .59,.84 ]; cluster 6 has .58 [ .24,.92 ]. Wide intervals signal substantial uncertainty. A ranking of point estimates is not a proven ranking of population performance.

steps.title: Use the comparison actually tested
steps.text: Figure 2.6 gives Tukey 95% family-wise intervals for pairwise differences. Under that procedure, cluster 5 is significantly below clusters 1, 2, 3 and 8. Overlap of two individual mean CIs is not the formal comparison rule.

steps.title: Read the limits of the model
steps.text: The report describes associations, with lifestyle and contextual confounding and model choices. Its regression output is not a simple unadjusted patient-mean comparison. In Table 2.3, stars do refer to stated p-value thresholds; a displayed p=0 is rounding, not literal zero.

cautions: Multiple comparisons need their stated family-wise procedure. Do not replace a Tukey difference interval with two unrelated 95% mean intervals.
No institutional configuration is established as universally best. An observational country association is not evidence that changing that feature alone causes the outcome.

questions.prompt: Cluster 2 has the highest displayed mean (.71). What can you conclude from that alone?
options: It is proven superior to every cluster
Its point estimate is largest; superiority needs appropriate comparisons and design
Its institutional features cause high efficiency
questions.explanation: A point estimate does not express comparison uncertainty or establish causality. Read the reported difference procedure.

questions.prompt: Which source supports a formal pairwise cluster comparison?
options: Whether separate mean intervals overlap
The order of rows in Table 2.1
The reported Tukey family-wise intervals for differences
questions.explanation: The report uses Tukey contrasts to address the family of comparisons. Individual mean CI overlap is not that test.

intervals.label: Cluster 1
intervals.meaning: Mean efficiency score .65, with published 95% CI [.48,.82].

intervals.label: Cluster 2
intervals.meaning: Mean .71 has the largest point estimate here, without by itself proving superiority.

intervals.label: Cluster 3
intervals.meaning: Mean .67 with considerable interval uncertainty.

intervals.label: Cluster 4
intervals.meaning: Mean .62; inspect difference intervals to compare clusters.

intervals.label: Cluster 5
intervals.meaning: Mean .21; reported Tukey contrasts identify specific significant differences.

intervals.label: Cluster 6
intervals.meaning: Mean .58 has a wide interval [.24,.92].

intervals.label: Cluster 7
intervals.meaning: Mean .64 with interval [.56,.71].

intervals.label: Cluster 8
intervals.meaning: The same rounded mean/interval as cluster 7 does not establish identical groups.

guides.intervalNote: Selected Table 2.1 mean intervals; these are not the Tukey intervals for differences in Figure 2.6. Plot is an original redraw of the selected numerical summaries.
